newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian shares rally, budget hopes overide politics.
newsitem.headline: Indian shares rally, budget hopes overide politics.

text.p: Indian equity markets clawed back more lost ground on Wednesday in the wake of the Congress party's weekend move to try to oust Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority coalition government.
Growing confidence that Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's widely acclaimed, investor-friendly budget would be salvaged out of the political mess shone through the gloom, dealers said.
The government has said it wants to pass the 1997/98 (April-March) budget, which was presented on February 28, before it faces a confidence vote on April 11.

President Shankar Dayal Sharma has given Deve Gowda until that date to prove his majority in parliament after the Congress party, the coalition's key ally, withdrew its support from the government on Sunday.
Bombay's benchmark index rallied another 3.25 percent on Wednesday, after gaining two percent on Tuesday.
The 30-share index closed up 111.38 points at 3,538.39. On Monday, the index fell 302 points, or about eight percent, its fourth largest plunge ever.

"What has emerged...is that there is a broad consensus amongst all political parties that it was a good budget and all efforts must be made to pass the budget," Tushar Sarda, president and chief executive at Daewoo Securities, told Reuters Financial Television.

Tampering with proposed corporate and personal tax cuts would alienate the business community and middle-income voters, which no party would want when chances for mid-term polls were so high, analysts said.

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the single largest group in the 545-member lower house of parliament, though short of an absolute majority, said the budget could be passed only after the confidence vote was first considered by parliament.
The Congress Party said it might seek unspecified changes before approving the budget.
"All politicians seem to believe that it would be political suicide to oppose the budget," a trader at a foreign institutional investor said.
But he said the market's optimism should be laced with caution while the government's fate remained unresolved.
"Sooner or later there will be a mid-term poll, and the fear will always be there," Alok Sethi, director of NatWest Markets in Bombay, said.
And he said there should be no rush to buy into India.
"The window of opportunity for investors to buy shares is going to be long and wide. This market is not going to run away," Sethi said.
A trader at a foreign brokerage said the market started climbing on Tuesday because of hopes the budget would go through. "That's uppermost on the market's mind," the trader said.
The National Stock Exchange top-50 index closed up 32.05 points, or 3.30 percent, at 1,002.20.
The Delhi index rallied strongly, gaining 25.63 points, or 3.5 percent, to close at 751.11 on Wednesday.
Deve Gowda's 15-member United Front coalition has 180 deputies, while the BJP and its allies have 193.
On Wednesday, the front page of the Hindu Business Line newspaper carried a cartoon of two men talking politics in a tea house.
"Whoever comes to power, I want them to prove their strength on the floor of the BSE," said one table-thumping character.
